column4: The source section's root ذ ك ر moves between public honor and inward remembrance; this ayah gives remembrance a reciprocal form, commanding people to remember God with the promise that He will remember them.

The section ends with desire turned toward the Lord and remembrance held inwardly; this ayah describes people calling their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face (يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِالْغَدَاةِ وَالْعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ), a specific form of that orientation.

This repeated caller scene says people call their Lord morning and evening desiring His face; it contrasts them with someone whose heart is heedless of God's remembrance and follows desire, sharpening the section's turn from public renown to inward longing.

This ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment; neighboring 16:7 describes animals carrying loads to distant lands, giving the section's saddle and caravan song a specific riding scene.

The section names bird and poultry cries as an animal branch of its sound image; Solomon says he was taught the speech of birds (مَنطِقَ الطَّيْرِ), a specific case where an animal voice carries intelligible speech.

An ant speaks and warns its community (قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ), and Solomon hears and smiles at her words; this gives the section's animal-sound detail a precise scene of a small creature's voice reaching a listener.

After hearing the ant in 27:18, Solomon turns to prayer, asking his Lord to enable gratitude (رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ); this joins the section's animal voice to its movement toward remembrance and praise.

The section hears words as sound and tracks what a listening ear receives; this ayah depicts people falling in prostration when the revealed verses are recited to them, a specific bodily response to voiced revelation.
Those listeners answer the recitation in 17:107 by glorifying their Lord (سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا); this is a spoken praise following heard revelation, matching the section's sense of ذكر as praise.
The listeners in 17:107 fall on their faces weeping and grow in humility; this ayah supplies the bodily response that completes the recitation scene, alongside the section's body-and-sound image.

The section's raised remembrance is meant to reach an ear; this ayah describes a covering over hearts and deafness in ears, then says that when the Lord alone is mentioned in the Quran, some turn away, a direct reversal of hearing.

The section ends with desire directed to the Lord; this ayah pictures people rising from their beds to call their Lord in fear and hope (يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ خَوْفًا وَطَمَعًا), giving that inward orientation a bodily and vocal setting.

The section compares a fine riding song with remembrance and prayer; this command to recite the Quran in measured recitation (وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا) gives a specific, deliberate mode of voiced sacred words.
